text: This lesson names a pattern you've actually seen several times already: the anonymous block. It's a PL-SQL block with no name, run directly, compiled and executed once, with nothing permanent created in the database.

Here's one. Set server output on, declare a count variable, select into it, print the result. Every block from Lesson 35 that wasn't attached to a create procedure or create function was already an anonymous block. It's the rough PL-SQL equivalent of opening SSMS, typing a few statements, and hitting execute, without ever wrapping them in a stored procedure.

D-B-M-S output dot put line is the tool you'll reach for constantly inside these blocks: printing a variable's value, confirming a branch of an if ran, tracing how far a script got. It's Oracle's rough equivalent of T-SQL's print statement — a debugging tool, not a way to return real result sets.

And here's the trip-up almost every T-SQL developer hits the first time: without set server output on, put line runs with absolutely no error, and yet nothing appears on screen, because the client tool only displays that buffered text once you've told it to. T-SQL's print has no equivalent toggle, which is exactly why this catches people off guard.

So when do you reach for an anonymous block instead of a real procedure? For the same situations where you'd already run a raw T-SQL batch instead of creating a stored procedure: ad hoc data fixes, one-time migrations, quick debugging. The moment the logic needs to be reusable or callable by other code, that's your signal to write a real named procedure instead.

Next lesson: REF CURSORs — the mechanism Oracle procedures actually need to hand back a genuine result set, since unlike T-SQL, a bare select inside an Oracle procedure doesn't automatically stream rows back to the caller. See you there.
